Formulation:
- Concise formulation integrating transcript and DDx:
  - Predisposing factors: Strong family history of migraine (mother and sister); female sex and age in typical range for migraine.
  - Precipitating factors: Recent increased work stress (new project), prolonged screen exposure, possible reduced hydration.
  - Perpetuating factors: Continued high screen exposure, possibly inadequate or incorrect use/dosing of OTC analgesics, no recent eye assessment despite long-term glasses use.
  - Protective factors: No red flag neurological features documented (no focal deficits, no fever, no vomiting), patient engaged and seeking care, social supports present.
  - Clinical interpretation: Presentation most consistent with an acute primary headache disorder — probable migraine (photophobia, transient visual phenomena, nausea, unilateral periorbital predominance, poor response to OTC ibuprofen) with contributory tension-type/eyestrain elements from occupational screen use. Serious secondary causes considered less likely given absence of sudden severe onset, focal deficits, fever, or neck stiffness; safety-netting and follow-up advised.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem: Probable acute migraine headache
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Rapid pain relief and reduction of headache severity.
  - Return to normal function/work without significant symptom recurrence.
  - Identify triggers and reduce future episodes.
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Provide effective acute analgesia and symptom control.
  - Exclude red-flag features and arrange further assessment if indicated.
  - Implement self-management strategies and monitoring (headache diary); consider prophylactic therapy only if recurrent.
- Actions (Patient):
  - Follow recommended analgesic strategy as advised by clinician (see clinician actions). Patient to clarify dosing with clinician/pharmacy.
  - Start a headache diary to record timing, severity, triggers (hydration, sleep, screen time, menses), and medication use.
  - Reduce screen brightness and take regular screen breaks (e.g., 20-20-20 rule) and ergonomic adjustments at work.
  - Optimize hydration and rest when symptomatic.
  - Seek urgent review or present to ED if new/worsening focal neurological signs, sudden severe (“thunderclap”) headache, persistent vomiting, fever, or visual loss.
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Offer/consider acute analgesic options (clinician discussed Naproxen; paracetamol; codeine-containing preparations). Note: dose/route/frequency not documented/prescribed in transcript — clinician to document prescription and dosing if initiated.
  - Clarify and document appropriate ibuprofen dosing if patient continues OTC (clinician advised up to two tablets three times a day — transcript provided that advice).
  - Provide counselling on red flags and safety-netting (return if worsening, new focal deficits, vision changes, weakness, persistent vomiting, fever).
  - Recommend headache diary and review in 1–2 weeks; consider starting prophylactic therapy if headaches become frequent/recurrent.
  - Recommend repeat eye test/optometry review to assess for refractive error or need for updated glasses.
  - If red flags arise or neurological signs develop, consider urgent neuroimaging or referral to ED/neurology per local protocols.

Secondary Problem: Tension-type headache / work-related eyestrain
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Reduce frequency of tension-type/headache related to screen use and stress.
  - Improve visual comfort during work.
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Address ergonomic and visual contributors; reduce screen-related strain.
  - Determine if corrective eyewear update is needed.
- Actions (Patient):
  - Implement regular breaks from screen work, adjust screen brightness and ergonomics, consider blue-light filters/anti-glare screens if helpful.
  - Schedule and attend optometry/eye test.
  - Use OTC analgesia per clinician guidance for interim symptomatic relief.
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Reinforce ergonomic advice and need for eye assessment.
  - Consider referral to optometry/ophthalmology if eye test identifies refractive issues or if visual symptoms persist despite correction.
  - Review effectiveness of workplace adjustments at follow-up.

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention:
- Education Given: Yes. Topics Covered:
  - Likely diagnosis (probable migraine), possible triggers (family history, stress, dehydration, screen use), acute treatment options, correct OTC dosing, headache diary, eye assessment, red flags warranting urgent review.
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening:
  - New or worsening focal neurological signs (weakness, speech changes), sudden severe headache, progressive visual loss, persistent vomiting, fever, decreased consciousness.
- Coping Strategies:
  - Headache diary, hydration, scheduled screen breaks and ergonomic measures, rest in a dark/quiet environment for acute attacks, adhere to advised analgesic plan, avoid frequent excessive analgesic use to prevent medication-overuse headache.

Consent, Coordination & Review:
- Patient Consent to Plan: Documented verbal agreement in transcript; patient accepted recommendations and follow-up.
- Copy of Mental Health Care Plan Given to Patient: Not recorded.
- Other Mental Health Professionals Involved in Patient Care: Not recorded.
- GP Acknowledgment (if completed by other MH Professional): Not recorded.
- Review Date: Recommended follow-up in 1–2 weeks; earlier if symptoms worsen or red flags develop.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Migraine headache (probable acute migraine) — Likelihood: High
  - Justification: Photophobia, transient visual phenomena ("shooting lights"), unilateral periorbital predominance, nausea/feeling sick, family history of migraine, severe pain (8/10), poor response to OTC ibuprofen.
- Tension-type headache / stress-related headache — Likelihood: Medium
  - Justification: Dull, diffuse pain; relation to prolonged screen use and recent work stress; prior headaches responsive to ibuprofen; does not fully account for photophobia/visual phenomena.
- Eyestrain / computer vision syndrome (refractive error–related headache) — Likelihood: Medium–Low
  - Justification: Longstanding glasses since childhood, high screen exposure with relief on reduced brightness; visual phenomena and systemic symptoms make this less likely as sole cause.
